---
title: "Scaling Test-Time Compute with Multi-Agent LLM Systems"
author:
  - name: Robert Yang
date: today
abstract: |
  Multi-agent LLM research matters because it is how we scale test-time compute beyond one agent's context window, memory, and serial reasoning path. A single agent can think longer, call more tools, and keep more notes, but only up to a point. Multi-agent systems can think wider: many attempts, tools, memories, branches, critiques, experiments, and checks. Classical multi-agent systems and multi-agent reinforcement learning had already shown that coordination is hard; modern LLM-agent systems changed the substrate. LLM calls became stateful, tool-using, artifact-producing workers that could be orchestrated at test time. The 2023 wave framed this possibility through artificial organizations: role-playing agents, social simulations, software companies, debate panels, and programmable conversations. The later empirical record is more selective. Interactive benchmarks, cost-aware evaluation, equal-budget controls, failure taxonomies, and long-horizon artifact studies show that more agents are not automatically better. Agent count is not a mechanism. Multi-agent systems help when they create useful search, complementary context, different tools or memories, checkable artifacts, credible verification, and better use of scarce human judgment. The newest turn makes coordination itself an optimization target: systems search over topology, routing, agent composition, and collaboration training rather than assuming roles and conversation are sufficient. This review argues that the durable form of modern multi-agent research is not "many chatbots talking," but coordinated test-time work: turning extra model calls, tools, memories, branches, critiques, and verifiers into reliable results that people can steer, audit, and use.
keywords:
  - LLM agents
  - multi-agent systems
  - test-time compute
  - orchestration
  - evaluation
  - verification
  - agent safety
---
